Geography is a hard one. The thing is that I don't think that given a map a lot of Europeans would be able to point out say, Kansas, on a map, or any number of states out side of California or Texas. America is such a massive country with states that have such vastly different cultures that in a lot of ways you could class them as being separate countries, sort of, apart from the fact that everyone speaks the same languages. That's the impression that I'm getting any way. So you can see how this insular mind set would occur. I think that most people in Europe are used to traveling over country barriers more than people in the US are. In addition to this I think that the problems are a lot closer in the geopolitical context, that is you tend to care what Russia does when they directly affect your gas bill.

The political situation is also hard, the impression that I get is that in America most presidential elections tend to come down to a number of key states that have always swung the balance of power. So the up shot of this is that unless you happen to live in one of these states then there really isn't that much point voting, at all. I think that this also has an effect on elections for the house or senate where things tend to be gerrymandered out to all fuck, as well. This isn't to say that other countries don't have this problem of the value of your vote depending on where you live, but I think that this is especially bad in the US than it is in other countries. This being reflected in the fact that politics in America is very right wing in nature since that's just where the vast majority of people who vote and whose vote counts live. That is there are obvious systematic problem with the American system that aren't going to be fixed anytime soon, because it just isn't for the benefit for the people in charge. In the same way that there are obvious problems with the British system that will never be changed either apart from platitudes and lip service to that effect.
